title: Were You There
origin: Traditional African American spiritual, likely predating the Civil War; first published 1899 in William E. Barton's Old Plantation Hymns
note: First printed in Barton's 1899 collection and corroborated by the Dictionary of North American Hymnology and Discipleship Ministries' History of Hymns as an anonymous spiritual of enslaved origin. The first spiritual admitted to a major U.S. denominational hymnal (Episcopal, 1940). Anonymous and public domain.
verses:
Were you there when they crucified my Lord?
Were you there when they crucified my Lord?
Oh, sometimes it causes me to tremble, tremble, tremble.
Were you there when they crucified my Lord?

Were you there when they nailed him to the tree?
Were you there when they nailed him to the tree?
Oh, sometimes it causes me to tremble, tremble, tremble.
Were you there when they nailed him to the tree?

Were you there when they pierced him in the side?
Were you there when they pierced him in the side?
Oh, sometimes it causes me to tremble, tremble, tremble.
Were you there when they pierced him in the side?

Were you there when the sun refused to shine?
Were you there when the sun refused to shine?
Oh, sometimes it causes me to tremble, tremble, tremble.
Were you there when the sun refused to shine?

Were you there when they laid him in the tomb?
Were you there when they laid him in the tomb?
Oh, sometimes it causes me to tremble, tremble, tremble.
Were you there when they laid him in the tomb?

title: Go Tell It on the Mountain
origin: Traditional African American spiritual; the refrain sung in Appalachia for years before the stanzas were written and the song first published by John Wesley Work Jr. in 1907 (Folk Songs of the American Negro)
note: Work Jr., the first Black collector of spirituals, supplied new stanzas for a much older, anonymous refrain whose original verses had been lost (per Wikipedia and the Times-Gazette hymn history). His 1907 publication places it firmly in the public domain.
verses:
Go, tell it on the mountain,
Over the hills and everywhere,
Go, tell it on the mountain,
That Jesus Christ is born.

While shepherds kept their watching
O'er silent flocks by night,
Behold, throughout the heavens
There shone a holy light.

The shepherds feared and trembled
When lo! above the earth
Rang out the angel chorus
That hailed our Savior's birth.

Down in a lowly manger
The humble Christ was born,
And God sent us salvation
That blessed Christmas morn.

title: Let Us Break Bread Together
origin: Traditional Gullah/Geechee spiritual of the South Carolina Sea Islands, some stanzas possibly dating to the 18th century; text first published 1925 in the Journal of American Folklore and in Nicholas Ballanta's Saint Helena Island Spirituals
note: Documented as an anonymous Gullah spiritual by two independent 1925 collections (Journal of American Folklore; Ballanta's Saint Helena Island Spirituals), and again in the Johnson brothers' Second Book of Negro Spirituals (1926). Anonymous and public domain.
verses:
Let us break bread together on our knees,
Let us break bread together on our knees,
When I fall on my knees with my face to the rising sun,
O Lord, have mercy on me.

Let us drink wine together on our knees,
Let us drink wine together on our knees,
When I fall on my knees with my face to the rising sun,
O Lord, have mercy on me.

Let us praise God together on our knees,
Let us praise God together on our knees,
When I fall on my knees with my face to the rising sun,
O Lord, have mercy on me.

title: St. Louis Blues
origin: W.C. Handy, published September 1914 by the Pace and Handy Music Company
note: Widely called the first published blues song to become a national hit. Confirmed public domain in the U.S. as a work published before 1930 (per Wikipedia's Saint Louis Blues entry and the 1914 sheet music held by the New York Public Library and Wikimedia Commons).
verses:
I hate to see the evening sun go down,
I hate to see the evening sun go down,
It makes me think I'm on my last go 'round.

Feeling tomorrow like I feel today,
Feeling tomorrow like I feel today,
I'll pack my trunk and make my getaway.

St. Louis woman with her diamond rings
Pulls that man around by her apron strings,
'Twere it not for powder and for store-bought hair,
The man I love would not have gone nowhere.

Got the St. Louis blues, just as blue as I can be,
That man's got a heart like a rock cast in the sea,
Or else he wouldn't have gone so far from me.

title: Beale Street Blues
origin: W.C. Handy, composed 1916 with words added 1917; self-published 1917 by Handy Bros. Music Co., New York
note: A tribute to the Memphis thoroughfare Handy knew from his early career. Confirmed public domain in the U.S. as a work published more than 95 years ago (per Wikipedia and the Library of Congress National Jukebox; original sheet music held by the LOC and NYPL).
verses:
I've seen the lights of gay Broadway,
Old Market Street down by the Frisco Bay,
I've strolled the Prado, I've gambled on the Bourse;
The seven wonders of the world I've seen,
And many are the places I have been.

You'll see pretty browns in beautiful gowns,
You'll see tailor-mades and hand-me-downs,
You'll meet honest men, and pickpockets skilled,
You'll find that business never closes till somebody gets killed.

If Beale Street could talk, if Beale Street could talk,
Married men would have to take their beds and walk,
Except one or two who never drink booze,
And the blind man on the corner who sings the Beale Street Blues.

I'd rather be here than any place I know,
I'd rather be here than any place I know,
It's gonna take the sergeant for to make me go.

title: Swannanoa Tunnel
origin: Traditional African American railroad work song from the construction of the Swannanoa Tunnel (completed March 1879) on the Western North Carolina Railroad; documented in the early 20th century by song collector Bascom Lamar Lunsford
note: Also known as 'Asheville Junction' and 'Swannanoa Town.' Sung by convict laborers, most of them Black men imprisoned under Jim Crow, who blasted the Blue Ridge tunnels in the 1870s; hundreds died in the work. Traditional and public domain.
verses:
Swannanoa Tunnel, all caved in,
Swannanoa Tunnel, all caved in,
Baby, all caved in.

I'm going back to the Swannanoa Tunnel,
That's my home, baby, that's my home.

Asheville Junction, Swannanoa Tunnel,
All caved in, baby, all caved in.

This old hammer, ring like silver,
Shine like gold, baby, shine like gold.

Take this hammer, throw it in the river,
I'll come back, baby, I'll come back.

When you hear my watchdog howling,
Somebody around, baby, somebody around.

title: Go Tell Aunt Rhody
origin: American folk song of 19th-century origin; the tune began as a gavotte in Jean-Jacques Rousseau's 1752 opera Le Devin du Village and entered U.S. hymnals as 'Greenville'/'Rousseau' around 1825
note: The melody predates the American verses by decades, having crossed from Rousseau's 1752 opera into English texts and hymnals before the folk lyric about the old gray goose attached to it. Ancient tune and 19th-century verses are both public domain.
verses:
Go tell Aunt Rhody,
Go tell Aunt Rhody,
Go tell Aunt Rhody,
The old gray goose is dead.

The one she's been saving,
The one she's been saving,
The one she's been saving,
To make a feather bed.

She died in the mill pond,
She died in the mill pond,
She died in the mill pond,
From standing on her head.

The goslings are crying,
The goslings are crying,
The goslings are crying,
Because their mother's dead.

The old gander's weeping,
The old gander's weeping,
The old gander's weeping,
Because his wife is dead.

title: Old MacDonald Had a Farm
origin: Traditional; earliest precursor is Thomas d'Urfey's 'In the Fields in Frost and Snow' (1706, revised 1719); the modern form was first printed as 'Ohio' in F.T. Nettleingham's Tommy's Tunes (1917)
note: Cecil Sharp collected a version ('The Farmyard') in 1908, and the Traditional Ballad Index cites the 1917 Tommy's Tunes text as the earliest of the modern form. The 18th-century roots and pre-1918 publication place it firmly in the public domain.
verses:
Old MacDonald had a farm, E-I-E-I-O,
And on that farm he had a cow, E-I-E-I-O,
With a moo-moo here and a moo-moo there,
Here a moo, there a moo, everywhere a moo-moo,
Old MacDonald had a farm, E-I-E-I-O.

Old MacDonald had a farm, E-I-E-I-O,
And on that farm he had a pig, E-I-E-I-O,
With an oink-oink here and an oink-oink there,
Here an oink, there an oink, everywhere an oink-oink,
Old MacDonald had a farm, E-I-E-I-O.

Old MacDonald had a farm, E-I-E-I-O,
And on that farm he had a duck, E-I-E-I-O,
With a quack-quack here and a quack-quack there,
Here a quack, there a quack, everywhere a quack-quack,
Old MacDonald had a farm, E-I-E-I-O.

Old MacDonald had a farm, E-I-E-I-O,
And on that farm he had a horse, E-I-E-I-O,
With a neigh-neigh here and a neigh-neigh there,
Here a neigh, there a neigh, everywhere a neigh-neigh,
Old MacDonald had a farm, E-I-E-I-O.

title: Early One Morning
origin: Traditional English folk song with 17th/18th-century roots; printed in the mid-19th century, including in William Chappell's Popular Music of the Olden Time (1855-1859)
note: A lament of an abandoned maiden, its fragments traceable to the 17th and 18th centuries and set in print by Victorian collectors such as Chappell. Traditional and public domain.
verses:
Early one morning, just as the sun was rising,
I heard a maid sing in the valley below;
Oh, don't deceive me, oh, never leave me,
How could you use a poor maiden so?

Remember the vows that you made to your Mary,
Remember the bower where you vowed to be true;
Oh, don't deceive me, oh, never leave me,
How could you use a poor maiden so?

Thus sang the poor maiden, her sorrows bewailing,
Thus sang the poor maid in the valley below;
Oh, don't deceive me, oh, never leave me,
How could you use a poor maiden so?

title: Santiana
origin: Traditional capstan shanty referencing the Mexican general Santa Anna and the Mexican-American War; dating from at least the 1850s, first printed in 1879
note: Also spelled 'Santy Anno.' Documented by Stan Hugill (Shanties from the Seven Seas, 1961) as dating to the Mexican-American War era; well attested from the 1860s onward with countless variant verses. Traditional and public domain.
verses:
Oh, Santiana gained the day,
Away, Santiana,
Santa Anna gained the day,
All on the plains of Mexico.

Oh, Santiana fought for gold,
Away, Santiana,
The deeds of Santy Anna told,
All on the plains of Mexico.

She's a fast clipper ship and a bully good crew,
Away, Santiana,
A down-east Yankee for her captain too,
All on the plains of Mexico.

Oh, Santy Anna's day is o'er,
Away, Santiana,
And Santy Anna will fight no more,
All on the plains of Mexico.

title: Roll the Cotton Down
origin: Traditional halyard and capstan shanty that originated among cotton-stowers and longshoremen of the American southern cotton ports; sung aboard ship by at least the 1870s
note: Documented in the collections of Williams (1909), Stanton H. King (1918), and Stan Hugill, who printed six distinct versions in Shanties from the Seven Seas. Carried from the cotton docks to deep water by seasonal stowers. Traditional and public domain.
verses:
Oh, a dollar a day is a stevedore's pay,
Roll the cotton down,
A dollar a day is a stevedore's pay,
Oh, roll the cotton down.

Away down south where I was born,
Roll the cotton down,
I worked in the cotton and I hoed the corn,
Oh, roll the cotton down.

Around Cape Horn we're bound to go,
Roll the cotton down,
Around Cape Horn through the ice and snow,
Oh, roll the cotton down.

Oh, rock and shake her is the cry,
Roll the cotton down,
The old man's wages are running high,
Oh, roll the cotton down.

title: Paddy Lay Back
origin: Traditional capstan shanty and forebitter, well known on British packet ships throughout the second half of the 19th century; in circulation by at least the late 1870s (Roud 653)
note: Also called 'Mainsail Haul.' Likely began as an Irish or English music-hall song before passing into the forecastle repertoire; described by Stan Hugill as especially popular in Liverpool ships. Traditional and public domain.
verses:
'Twas a cold and dreary morning in December,
And all of my money it was spent,
Where it went to, Lord, I can't remember,
So down to the shipping office went.

Paddy, lay back! Paddy, lay back!
Take in your slack, take a turn around the capstan, heave a pawl,
About ship's stations, boys, be handy,
For we're bound for Valparaiso round the Horn.

That day there was a great demand for sailors,
For the Colonies and for 'Frisco and for France,
So I shipped aboard a Limey barque, the Hotspur,
And got paralytic drunk on my advance.

Now I joined her on a cold December morning,
A-frapping of my flippers to keep me warm,
With the south cone a-hoisted as a warning,
To stand by the coming of a storm.

title: Edward
origin: Traditional Scottish ballad, Child Ballad No. 13; first printed in Bishop Thomas Percy's Reliques of Ancient English Poetry (1765), from a manuscript supplied by Sir David Dalrymple
note: A grim question-and-answer ballad in which a mother draws from her son the confession that he has killed his father. One of the most admired of the Child ballads; Franz Schubert set a German translation. Ancient and public domain.
verses:
'Why does your brand so drop with blood,
Edward, Edward?
Why does your brand so drop with blood,
And why so sad go ye, O?'
'O I have killed my hawk so good,
Mother, mother,
O I have killed my hawk so good,
And I had no more but he, O.'

'Your hawk's blood was never so red,
Edward, Edward,
Your hawk's blood was never so red,
My dear son, I tell thee, O.'
'O I have killed my red-roan steed,
Mother, mother,
O I have killed my red-roan steed,
That once was so fair and free, O.'

'Why does your brand so drop with blood,
Edward, Edward?
Some other grief you suffer, O.'
'O I have killed my father dear,
Mother, mother,
O I have killed my father dear,
Alas, and woe is me, O!'

'And what penance will ye do for that,
Edward, Edward?'
'I'll set my feet in yonder boat,
Mother, mother,
And I'll fare over the sea, O.'

title: Mary Hamilton
origin: Traditional Scottish ballad, Child Ballad No. 173 (Roud 79), dating to the 16th century and associated with the court of Mary, Queen of Scots
note: Also known as 'The Four Marys.' Sung by a condemned lady-in-waiting on the eve of her execution; historians link it to a confusion of a Scottish court scandal with a similar 1719 case at the court of Peter the Great. Ancient and public domain.
verses:
Word's gane to the kitchen,
And word's gane to the ha',
That Marie Hamilton gangs wi' bairn
To the highest Stewart of a'.

'Oh, little did my mother think,
The day she cradled me,
What lands I was to travel through,
What death I was to dee.'

'Yestreen the Queen had four Maries,
The night she'll hae but three,
There was Marie Seaton, and Marie Beaton,
And Marie Carmichael, and me.'

'Oh, happy, happy is the maid,
That's born of beauty free,
It was my dimpling rosy cheeks
That's been the ruin o' me.'

title: Earl Brand (The Douglas Tragedy)
origin: Traditional Scottish/English ballad, Child Ballad No. 7, with roots in older Scandinavian ballad tradition; the Scottish 'Douglas Tragedy' form was localized to Selkirkshire and printed in the early 19th century
note: A ballad of an elopement that ends in the deaths of the lovers and the bride's pursuing kin, closing with the rose-and-briar motif also found in 'Barbara Allen.' Ancient and public domain.
verses:
'Rise up, rise up, now, Lord Douglas,' she says,
'And put on your armour so bright,
Let it never be said that a daughter of thine
Was married to a lord under night.'

He's mounted her on a milk-white steed,
And himself on a dapple grey,
With a bugelet horn hung down by his side,
And lightly they rode away.

Lord William looked o'er his left shoulder,
To see what he could see,
And there he spied her seven brethren bold,
Come riding over the lea.

'Light down, light down, Lady Margaret,' he said,
'And hold my steed in your hand,
Until that against your seven brethren bold,
And your father, I make a stand.'

title: Clerk Saunders
origin: Traditional Scottish ballad, Child Ballad No. 69, collected in Scotland and printed by Walter Scott in Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border (1802-1803)
note: A tragic ballad in which a young man is slain in his sleep by one of his lover's brothers, then returns as a ghost to release her from her vows. Ancient and public domain.
verses:
Clerk Saunders and May Margaret
Walked owre yon garden green,
And sad and heavy was the love
That fell thir twa between.

'A bed, a bed,' Clerk Saunders said,
'A bed for you and me!'
'Fye na, fye na,' said May Margaret,
'Till anes we married be.'

Then in and came her seven brothers,
Wi' torches burning bright,
They said, 'We hae but one sister,
And here she's lying wi' a knight.'

Then out and spake the seventh o' them,
His words were said in scorn,
'It's I will bear the brand,' he said,
'Shall gar Clerk Saunders die.'

title: Let Me Call You Sweetheart
origin: Words by Beth Slater Whitson, music by Leo Friedman; published 1910 by the Harold Rossiter Music Company, Chicago
note: A massive hit for the Peerless Quartet in 1911 and an enduring barbershop standard. Confirmed public domain as a work published in 1910 (per Wikipedia, the Songwriters Hall of Fame, and the sheet music held by the Smithsonian and Library of Congress).
verses:
I am dreaming, dear, of you,
Day by day,
Dreaming when the skies are blue,
When they're gray;
When the silv'ry moonlight gleams,
Still I wander on in dreams,
In a land of love, it seems,
Just with you.

Let me call you sweetheart, I'm in love with you,
Let me hear you whisper that you love me too,
Keep the love-light glowing in your eyes so true,
Let me call you sweetheart, I'm in love with you.

title: By the Light of the Silvery Moon
origin: Music by Gus Edwards, lyrics by Edward Madden; published 1909 by Jerome H. Remick & Co.
note: Introduced in the Ziegfeld Follies of 1909 and a hit on record in 1910. Confirmed public domain as a work published in 1909 (per Wikipedia, the Public Domain Review, and the sheet music held by the NYPL and university collections).
verses:
Place park, scene dark, silv'ry moon is shining through the trees,
Cast two, me, you, sound of kisses floating on the breeze.

By the light of the silvery moon,
I want to spoon,
To my honey I'll croon love's tune,
Honey moon, keep a-shining in June,
Your silvery beams will bring love's dreams,
We'll be cuddling soon,
By the silvery moon.

Act two, scene new, roses blooming all around the place,
Cast three, you, me, preacher with a solemn face.

title: Alexander's Ragtime Band
origin: Words and music by Irving Berlin; copyrighted March 18, 1911, and published the same year by Ted Snyder Co.
note: Berlin's breakthrough hit, selling millions of copies of sheet music and helping launch the ragtime craze. Confirmed public domain in the U.S. as a 1911 publication (per Wikipedia, History.com, and the Library of Congress National Jukebox).
verses:
Oh, ma honey, oh, ma honey,
Better hurry and let's meander,
Ain't you goin', ain't you goin',
To the leader man, ragged meter man?
Oh, ma honey, oh, ma honey,
Let me take you to Alexander's
Grand stand, brass band,
Ain't you comin' along?

Come on and hear, come on and hear,
Alexander's Ragtime Band,
Come on and hear, come on and hear,
It's the best band in the land,
They can play a bugle call like you never heard before,
So natural that you want to go to war,
That's just the bestest band what am, honey lamb.

Come on along, come on along,
Let me take you by the hand,
Up to the man, up to the man,
Who's the leader of the band,
And if you care to hear the Swanee River played in ragtime,
Come on and hear, come on and hear,
Alexander's Ragtime Band.

title: Come Josephine in My Flying Machine
origin: Music by Fred Fisher, lyrics by Alfred Bryan; published October 18, 1910, by Shapiro Music
note: A hit celebrating the new age of flight, introduced by Blanche Ring and later sung by Jack in the 1997 film Titanic. Confirmed public domain as a 1910 publication (per Wikipedia, the Smithsonian, and the Library of Congress National Jukebox).
verses:
Oh, say, let us fly, dear,
Where, kid? To the sky, dear,
Oh, you flying machine,
Jump in, Miss Josephine,
Ship ahoy! Oh, joy, what a feeling,
Where, boy? In the ceiling,
Ho, high, hoopla, we fly
To the sky so high.

Come Josephine, in my flying machine,
Going up she goes! Up she goes!
Balance yourself like a bird on a beam,
In the air she goes! There she goes!
Up, up, a little bit higher,
Oh, my! The moon is on fire,
Come Josephine, in my flying machine,
Going up, all on, goodbye!

One, two, now we rise, dear,
Up, up to the skies, dear,
Whirled through the clouds we go,
While all the crowds below
Can't see us at all, so high we fly,
Up in the deep blue sky,
And we'll swing and we'll sway
Till the break of day.
